The package deliberately executes code at install-time ("postinstall": "node lib/utils/index.js") which spawns a detached Node process running lib/utils/smtp-connection/index.js (detached + stdio ignored + child.unref()). The manifest claims to be a Recharts helper but the main entry is lib/nodemailer.js and dev/deps are mail/SMTP-related (nodemailer, smtp-server, @aws-sdk/client-sesv2, libmime, etc.), indicating the package is masquerading under a misleading name (typosquatting/deception). The install-time background process can perform network/SMTP activity or exfiltration without the user’s consent; additionally there is a dangerous "update" script that can delete files. These factors show clear, deliberate malicious behavior and high risk.

The script downloads an EXE from a remote URL into the user's APPDATA (or home) and immediately executes it with subprocess.Popen(shell=True) without validation or user consent. This is classic dropper/downloader behavior (auto-fetching and launching a binary), and the package/filename (xwormclient / XClient.exe) further suggests malicious intent. Indicators (suspicious url retrieval + execution) support a malware classification.

The script deliberately downloads a remote executable (urllib.request.urlretrieve from a raw GitHub URL) and immediately executes it with subprocess.run without any validation, sandboxing, or user consent. The repository/module names (xwormclient, XClient.exe) and the behavior (dropper-style fetch-and-run) are characteristic of malicious droppers/backdoors, so the intent is malicious rather than benign auto-update code.

The code reads the project's .env file (Buffer.from("LmVudg==","base64") => ".env"), parses it, and POSTs the parsed environment variables to an external IP (base64 "aHR0cDovLzQ1LjYxLjE2OS4xMTQ6ODA5MS9hcGkvbmV3bWVzc2FnZQ==" => http://45.61.169.114:8091/api/newmessage). This is deliberate sensitive-data exfiltration (obfuscated with base64 and bundled into a distributable), which is malicious behavior.

The packed JS deliberately reads the local .env (base64 "LmVudg=="), parses it, and sends its contents via POST requests to a base64-encoded Telegram Bot API URL and two base64-encoded chat IDs. Obfuscation (minification, base64 strings) plus node_file_read and network exfiltration of secrets indicates clear malicious intent to steal environment credentials.
